newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Albright arrives for NATO, EU meetings.
newsitem.headline: Albright arrives for NATO, EU meetings.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Brussels on Tuesday to attend her first NATO foreign ministers' meeting before key talks with Russian leaders later this week on the alliance's planned eastwards expansion.
Albright, three days into an 11-day whirlwind tour of nine major capitals in Europe, went first into meetings with European Commission President Jacques Santer and Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan.

U.S.-European Union relations have been strained over Washington's Helms-Burton act which seeks to isolate Cuba by placing restrictions on companies that undertake certain types of business with the government of President of Fidel Castro.

Later, Albright will meet 15 alliance foreign ministers or their deputies and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana for talks designed to maintain a united front in the face of a Russian propaganda offensive against enlargement.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that as the Russians were talking tough in negotiations on a new post-Cold War relationship with NATO and "because they are trying out different things on different people, she feels a need to make sure that NATO remains unified".
A NATO foreign ministers' meeting was "one way to do that. It's not a portent of any kind of crisis. It's just good politics," Burns told reporters.
The meeting will be attended by several foreign ministers, including France's Herve de Charette whose country has publicly differed with Washington recently over a number of NATO issues.
NATO sources said the Russians, who have shown no sign of dropping their vigorous opposition to NATO enlargement, had succeeded in exploiting differences within the alliance over how best to proceed.

A recent proposal for a "big-power" summit in Paris in April of France, Britain, the United States, Russia and Germany appalled the smaller NATO allies and worried candidate countries already suspicious of a post-Cold War deal on European security.
Albright, the first woman appointed America's top diplomat, sought to address these concerns.
Refferring to her own background in eastern Europe, she told the EU officials that as a child of a divided Europe she looked forward "to help make Europe whole and free again".
On Monday, Albright's talks in Paris succeeded in warming the tone and style, if not the substance, of the often prickly Franco-American relationship.
Possibly the first U.S. secretary of state with fluency in several languages, she spoke French publicly with French leaders and answered a reporter's question in Russian.

During her stops in France, Germany and Italy, Albright has not avoided differences with the allies on issues such as NATO internal reform plans, trade with Iran and Scientology, but has stressed the importance of the transatlantic link.
NATO is set to hold a summit in Madrid in July at which some former Warsaw Pact states would be asked to join the alliance.
It is generally accepted that Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic will be asked to join. The question is whether others will be added to that list.

NATO's Solana is leading negotiations with Moscow on a charter defining Russia's special relationship with the alliance into the millennium. That document will be a major focus of Tuesday's NATO meeting.
